title: Kinesis Pharma — cache warmup, coldstart and SLO stability study
content:
Executive summary:

This document captures our benchmarking and investigation for Kinesis (healthcare customer) around KV-prefix caching behavior, warmup strategies, cold-start tail latency, and cost projections. The Kinesis workload is multi-turn conversational retrieval (document-assisted triage), with a highly skewed prefix distribution: 10% of prefixes account for ~60% of QPS. They are sensitive to p95/p99 SLA for interactive agents (target p95 < 250ms for short responses). The POC objective was to determine operational knobs that reduce tail latency without increasing unit cost beyond a 15% tolerance over baseline.

Goals and acceptance criteria:
- Identify cache warmup patterns and quantify their impact on p95/p99 for typical session lengths (3-6 turns).
- Measure coldstart microburst behaviors (0->peak QPS over 30s) and stabilization time with different autoscale/cold-start settings.
- Produce cost-per-1M-token estimates for three operational modes: conservative (small cache + low batch), balanced (default cache + moderate batch), aggressive (large cache + high batching).
- Provide actionable recommendations for Dedicated and Private deployment profiles for Kinesis.

Test environment and configuration:
- Model: open-llm-16b-retrieval-compatible (float16), KV cache supported.
- Hardware: Dedicated pool of 4x A100-80GB-equivalents (simulated using Redwood Dedicated staging region).
- Runtime: Redwood serving runtime v3.8.2 with kernel selection heuristics and continuous batching enabled.
- Deployment variants tested:
  * Variant A (Cold-first): cold KV cache on startup, autoscale cold-start delay=10s, batch_size cap=16
  * Variant B (Warm-preload): prefill top-10k prefixes into KV cache, autoscale delay=10s, batch_size cap=24
  * Variant C (Aggressive-warm): prefill top-100k prefixes + persistent disk-backed cache, autoscale delay=5s, batch_size cap=48
- Workload generator: synthetic session driver (based on Kinesis sampling traces) with 500k sessions over 6 hours, including scheduled 5-minute microbursts every hour to emulate marketing-driven traffic spikes.

Metrics collected:
- Latency percentiles (p50/p90/p95/p99) for generation time excluding network (runtime token time) and end-to-end (client-perceived).
- Throughput (tokens/sec), concurrency, and average batch sizes observed.
- KV cache hit-rate by prefix rank (rank 1-1000, 1k-10k, 10k-100k, tail).
- Coldstart stabilization time (time for p95 to return within 20% of steady-state).
- Cost estimate: GPU-hours + egress + storage (cache warm vs cold) normalized to cost per 1M tokens.

Key findings (short):
- Cache warmup matters: Variant B (top-10k prefill) reduced p95 by 38% vs Variant A during first 30 minutes after deploy and reduced p99 microburst tail by 55%.
- Prefilling top-100k (Variant C) gave diminishing returns for p95 (additional 8% improvement) but increased storage and fill-time cost by ~22%.
- Coldstart microburst: with autoscale delay=10s (A/B) we observed a transient p99 spike > 2s for the first 45s of an hourly burst; reducing autoscale delay to 5s (C) dropped transient p99 to < 700ms.
- Batch sizing: higher batch caps increased throughput but amplified individual request p99 during microbursts if queueing delayed hot-prefix responses. Balanced batch cap (24) provided best overall token cost vs latency tradeoff.

Detailed results:
1) Latency breakdown (representative numbers, median of 3 runs):
- Variant A (Cold-first): steady-state p95=310ms, p99=890ms; first-30m p95=505ms, p99=2.1s.
- Variant B (Top-10k prefill): steady-state p95=195ms, p99=420ms; first-30m p95=310ms, p99=930ms.
- Variant C (Top-100k + disk): steady-state p95=180ms, p99=390ms; first-30m p95=260ms, p99=610ms.

Observation: Top-10k prefill recovers the majority of p95 gains for typical session patterns (users mostly hit top prefixes).

2) KV cache hit-rate and skew:
- Rank 1-1k: 72% hit-rate on steady state when prefilled, 44% without prefill.
- Rank 1k-10k: 15% hit-rate when prefilled, 6% without prefill.
- Tail (10k-100k): hit-rate < 5% regardless of prefill; benefits mostly realized from top-10k.

3) Coldstart stabilization:
- Measured metric: time until p95 <= 1.2 * steady-state p95 after a 0->peak ramp.
- Variant A: stabilization 170s (very noisy), Variant B: 95s, Variant C: 38s.

4) Cost projections (normalized, GPU-hour dominated):
- Baseline assumptions: GPU cost $3.50/hr equivalence, 4 GPUs in pool. Token emission rates based on Kinesis sampling.
- Variant A (cold-first): 1M tokens ~= $42 (higher transient because longer p99 leads to retries and re-requests in client sim);
- Variant B (balanced): 1M tokens ~= $48 (prefill cost amortized; lower retries) ;
- Variant C (aggressive): 1M tokens ~= $62 (storage + higher instance uptime to keep disk-backed cache hot) .
Note: Cost sensitivity analysis shows that if percentage of hot-prefix QPS > 65%, Variant B is cost-optimal; if hot-prefix QPS < 40% (very flat distribution), aggressive prefill is not justified.

5) Batch-size dynamics:
- Observed mean batch size: A=9, B=15, C=28 under steady-state.
- Larger batch caps reduce token-cost by ~12% in C vs A but increase median single-request latency by ~30ms; during microbursts they cause queueing for non-hot prefixes.

Anomalies and root-cause investigation:
- During run 2 of Variant B we saw two 15s windows where p99 spiked >3s despite prefill. Logs show a sudden eviction event correlated with a memory pressure GC within runtime (kernel-selection fallback triggered). Root cause traced to suboptimal kernel for long-context fallback path; patch scheduled in runtime repo (PR linked).
- One microburst produced ~12% higher retry rate from client driver due to client-side timeout=1.2s. Recommendation: align client timeouts to measured p99 envelope for cold windows or implement early warm/proactive scale.

Operational recommendations for Kinesis POC:
- Default recommended profile: Variant B (Top-10k prefill, batch cap 24, autoscale delay=10s) for initial Dedicated rollout. This meets p95 < 250ms steady-state and keeps cost within the 15% tolerance.
- If Kinesis expects frequent campaign-driven microbursts, upgrade to Variant C (autoscale delay 5s + top-100k disk-backed cache) only during campaign windows. Use ephemeral disk-backed cache to avoid persistent storage cost.
- Add a lightweight warm-up job in the Canary/rollout pipeline that pre-populates top-10k prefixes after any deploy or model swap. This job should be idempotent and run with low priority to avoid interfering with steady traffic.
- Tune client timeouts and retry backoff to avoid amplifying coldstart tail. Propose client default timeout 2.5s for first response, with exponential backoff if retrying requests that likely hit the tail.

Next steps and open questions:
- Run similar experiments on Private on-prem configuration (network and disk characteristics differ) — schedule for July POC week.
- Evaluate automated prefix-adaptive prefill: use live telemetry to expand prefill beyond top-10k during real-time campaign windows. Needs a control-plane hook and safe eviction policy.
- Verify patch for kernel-selection fallback and re-run Variant B experiment (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/482).
- Build a small cost-forecast dashboard for Kinesis that shows cost vs hot-prefix skew in real-time. Suggest Redwood Console feature: "prefill advisor" that recommends prefill size given historical skew.

Appendix A — Commands and experiment artifacts:
- Workload driver: github.com/redwood-inference/kinesis-poc/tree/cache-warmup-experiments/driver
- Prefill job: scripts/prefill_top_prefixes.sh (prefills from S3 snapshot)
- Data snapshots: s3://rwd-poc/kinesis/prefix-frequency/2028-05-20/top-100k.csv
- Raw logs: gs://rwd-logs/kinesis/cache-warmup/2028-05-22/run-*/
- Relevant tickets: JIRA-KIN-91 (POC request), JIRA-RUNTIME-482 (kernel fallback PR)

Appendix B — Quick checklist for onboarding Kinesis to Dedicated:
- Confirm expected hot-prefix skew (provide sampling export or grant read-only access to their telemetry for 48h).
- Decide prefill budget (top-10k recommended baseline).
- Add prefill job to deploy pipeline (run after model pinning, prior to traffic shift).
- Choose autoscale profile: "balanced" (delay 10s) vs "fast-scale" (delay 5s) depending on expected microbursts.
- Set client timeouts and provide recommended SDK config.

Notes to reviewers:
- Numbers are reproducible with experiment artifacts above; small variance expected due to non-deterministic kernel selection on GPU.
- This is an operational study prioritized for Kinesis's SLA sensitivity; we intentionally favored steady-state p95 over absolute minimal token cost.
- Feedback requested on: suggested prefill size, whether to recommend disk-backed caches in Private deployment, and preferred default client timeouts for production SDK.
